lines.text: Don't buy another coding course until you watch this.
Only about three out of every hundred people finish the online courses they start.
It's not because they're lazy. It's the design. And games solved this years ago.
Here are the five tricks games use to keep you playing, and how they help you finish learning.
First, why you quit. A course gives you hours and hours of video, one huge finish line, and nobody who notices when you stop.
Day one feels great. Day five, you skip. Day twelve, you forget it exists.
Harvard and MIT studied millions of learners. In the latest year they looked at, just over three percent finished.
Trick one. Tiny levels. A game never asks you to play for forty hours. It gives you one level. A few minutes. Then a win.
Every win is a small hit of progress, so you want the next one.
Trick two. The streak. A number that grows every day you show up.
Your brain hates losing something more than it likes winning it. Psychologists call that loss aversion.
So once you have a streak, you protect it. Duolingo says learners who hit a seven day streak are three point six times more likely to finish their course.
Trick three. The progress bar. In one famous study, a coffee shop handed out cards. Buy ten, get one free.
The closer people got to the free coffee, the faster they bought. It's called the goal gradient.
Games use it everywhere. Quests. Chests. Bars that are almost full.
But tricks alone won't keep you going for months. The last two will.
Quick thing. Every trick in this video is built into Teyro.
Lessons, streaks, quests and leagues, for coding and AI. Okay. Trick four.
Other players. Games put you on a leaderboard with real people.
Now you're not studying alone. You're racing the person just above you. And your friends notice when you skip.
Trick five. Rewards you earn. Coins. Chests. A shop to spend them in.
But the reward isn't the point. It's a reason to come back tomorrow, until coming back is just a habit.
Here's the catch. Most games are built to keep you playing forever. A good learning game is built so you finish.
The tricks only matter if every lesson makes you actually do something. Write the code. Fix the bug. Get it right.
To be fair, no app can learn for you. You still have to show up. The trick is making showing up easy.
So. Tiny levels. A streak. A progress bar. Other players. Rewards. That's how games keep you coming back.

Follow friends, race their streaks, and join your course community.
It feels like playing. But you finish.
